meta.title: Skills. Build and Use — course 2 · AIVIS.ONE
meta.desc: A free AIVIS.ONE course: how to build your own skill for a repeating task, run it and check it.
s01.t03: In this course you will learn to
s01.t04: take someone else's skill apart into five elements
s01.t05: build your own skill for a repeating task and run it on 3–5 tasks
s01.t06: check it with checkit and fixit and reach the verdict “clean”
s02.t02: A skill is a briefing, a prompt is a one-off request
s02.t04: “Write an announcement for the book exchange on Saturday”
s02.t05: You write it again every time, and every time the announcement comes out different.
s02.t08: date, place, theme, what to bring
s02.t10: the order of steps is written down once
s02.t12: an announcement in the same template
s02.t13: A prompt is work every time. A skill is an agreement written down once: you call it with one line.
s03.t02: The ladder: skill, workplace, agent, strict order of work (protocol)
s03.t07: Rules for one type of task
s03.t08: a set of your own skills covers your repeating tasks
s03.t10: A place where the assistant sees your real files and folders (in course 3 this is “an assistant on your computer”)
s03.t11: you regularly work with files and projects
s03.t13: A chat you gave a role and a task that carries out the steps itself and picks the right skill
s03.t14: you often run a long process of many steps
s03.t16: Written rules for a project: which documents to keep, how work is accepted, who decides what
s03.t17: the project runs through many chats
s03.t18: Do not climb for the sake of the ladder: a skill you use every day beats an agent you do not trust.
s03.t19: A skill is an ordinary text file. Where you add it depends on your chat.
s04.t02: The five elements of a skill
s04.t03: Role: who the model (the program that writes the chat's answers) is in this task and from whose point of view it looks.
s04.t04: Context: what the model must know about your field: words, nuances. This is where your skill differs from someone else's.
s04.t05: Procedure: the order of steps: first this, then that.
s04.t06: Output template: the exact shape of the result: sections, order, length.
s04.t07: Criteria: what counts as a good result and what to avoid.
s04.t08: One element missing, and the skill breaks at exactly that spot.
s05.t02: Take someone else's skill apart in five steps
s05.t03: Open any ready-made skill (for example the gift on slide 10) and find the five elements.
s05.t04: Read between the lines: the role may sit in the first sentence, the criteria in the examples.
s05.t05: Run it on a piece of your own real data.
s05.t06: Compare it with how you would have done it yourself.
s05.t07: Mark the differences: those are the places to adapt the skill to yourself.
s05.t08: After taking a few skills apart you start to see the pattern, and building your own gets easier.
s06.t02: Is the task ripe: five signs
s06.t03: It repeats: you do it again and again.
s06.t04: The shape is stable: input and result look alike every time.
s06.t05: The request costs time: every time you spend long wording it.
s06.t07: You can explain to a beginner how to do it well.
s06.t08: One skill, one task. Three tasks, three skills one after another; split a long input into parts.
s07.t03: Retell: state the task in your own words and write down the assumptions.
s07.t04: Sample requests: two or three, in the words you yourself would use to ask for it.
s07.t05: Name: short, in Latin letters, no spaces (for example book-exchange-announcement).
s07.t06: Description: what the skill does and when to use it.
s07.t07: Rules: the points of the procedure and criteria, no more than six, each with its reason.
s07.t08: Our skill: input is date, place, theme, what to bring; output is an announcement in one template.
s08.t01: What a skill file looks like
s08.t02: What is inside and how to name it
s08.t07: One text file. Name it SKILL.md (“.md” is just the ending of the name)
s08.t10: First line: the word name:, a space and a short name. These two words are typed exactly like this, in English; the ready skill on slides 10 and 11 already has them, you only replace the text after them.
s08.t11: Latin letters, no spaces, up to 64 characters
s08.t13: Second line: the word description:, a space and one or two sentences: what the skill does and when to use it
s08.t14: up to 1024 characters (about ten lines); use the words you would say yourself
s08.t15: The chat always sees a skill's name and description. It reads the rest of the text when the skill is needed: you called it by name, or the description fits the conversation.
s09.t02: Six steps to build, a check at each
s09.t03: One sentence: what comes in, what comes out. It does not fit: too early to build.
s09.t04: The procedure in words, as you do it yourself: every step a concrete action.
s09.t05: Two or three examples: a real input and the ideal result.
s09.t06: Criteria: “must have this, must not have that”, checkable by eye.
s09.t07: The file: all five elements in place.
s09.t08: Test runs on real tasks: run, find the weak spot, edit.
s10.t02: Your first skill, step by step
s10.t03: A small working skill: it asks the design questions, assembles the five elements, proposes 3–5 test runs and names the typical mistakes
s11.t03: Copy the text, save it as a file named SKILL.md and add it to your chat: in the settings look for a section called “Skills”, “Projects” or similar (the name varies). If there is none, paste the text at the start of the chat. The first lines between the three dashes are the skill's “business card” (name and description); leave them as they are. Run it: give the four fields, date, place, theme, what to bring. The text stays in English; the skill answers in the language of your fields.
s11.p01:
---
name: book-exchange-announcement
description: "Writes an announcement for a book exchange event from fixed fields: date, place, theme, what to bring. Use when the user gives event details and asks for an announcement, a notice, a poster text or an invitation post for a book exchange."
---

# Book exchange announcement

Role: you are an organiser who writes short, friendly notices for neighbours and colleagues.

Context: a book exchange is a small event where people swap books they have read. The input is four fields: date, place, theme, what to bring.

Steps:
1. Check that all four fields are present. If one is missing, ask for it and stop.
2. Write the announcement in the template below.
3. Check it against the criteria and fix what fails.

Template (four lines):
Title: the theme, one line
Date and place: one line
What to bring: one line
Invitation: one closing line

Criteria: all four fields appear as given; no more than five lines; no exclamation marks; no invented facts; written in the language of the fields.
s12.t03: Predict: before the run, write down what the skill should do.
s12.t04: Run it in a fresh chat that sees only the skill and your case.
s12.t05: Compare: what you expected and what you got; quote the difference word for word.
s12.t06: Find the cause: a fault in the file (something is missing) or a fault in the answer (the file is fine but the model did not follow it).
s12.t07: Edit and repeat on tasks of different difficulty: simple, medium, hard, unusual.
s12.t08: One good run is not a test.
s13.t02: Does the skill get called on time: “should” and “should not”
s13.t06: “Make an announcement: book exchange, Saturday, 12:00, the courtyard”
s13.t09: “Write an invitation post for a book swap: here are the date and place”
s13.t11: the same job in other words
s13.t12: “Make a preparation plan for the book exchange”
s13.t14: a near miss: same theme, different job
s13.t15: “Write an advert for selling a bicycle”
s13.t17: the same word, a different job
s13.t18: It starts on a “no” or stays silent on a “yes”: edit the description, because that is what calls the skill.
s14.t02: “Be careful” does not work: ask for a checkable action
s14.t05: It can be “done” in the head, and the model sincerely believes it was.
s14.t08: “Name three places where the skill can fail”
s14.t10: “Quote the line before you judge it”
s14.t12: “Find what is broken”, not “confirm it is fine”
s14.t13: The author does not sign off their own work: a model leans toward approving what it just made.
s15.t07: A rough sketch, a few lines
s15.t08: Find wrong facts, gaps, drift from the task; say what cannot be verified
s15.t11: Re-read it whole, find what was agreed but did not reach the text, mark “needs checking”
s15.t13: A skill others will use, several files, or any doubt
s15.t14: A list of every claim, severity marks: SERIOUS (stops the work), MISSED (does not stop it, but something needed is absent), MINOR (cosmetic), logic errors, up to three rounds of checking
s15.t15: In doubt, take the full one. A skill you will share gets an independent check with checkit.
s16.t03: checkit finds and does not fix; fixit fixes and does not confirm; a second audit says clean. These are two skill texts: add each one as on slide 11 and give it your own skill to check.
s16.t04: checkit: hunts for defects, edits nothing, gives a verdict.
s16.t05: fixit: repairs only what was found and never declares “clean”.
s17.t02: A skill with two defects: the find, the fix, the verdict
s17.t04: The course authors planted two errors in a practice skill in advance. checkit found both and several more: 1 mark SERIOUS (the template has no “what to bring” slot the steps rely on), 3 marks MISSED (one of them a description with no words a user would type), 4 marks MINOR.
s17.t06: fixit added the “what to bring” slot, rewrote the description with the words “announcement”, “invitation” and a sample request, and set rules for missing fields. It did not certify its own work.
s17.t08: A separate checkit run: “clean” (meaning no SERIOUS or MISSED, only minor points left) — 0 SERIOUS, 0 MISSED, 4 MINOR. One thing only a live run shows: does the skill get called. That is your task: add it the same way as on slide 11 and ask “write an announcement for our book exchange on Saturday”.
s17.t09: The cycle: checkit finds, fixit fixes, a second audit confirms.
s18.t02: Pitfalls and a checklist before sharing
s18.t03: A weak description: it lacks the words that get the skill called.
s18.t04: More than six rules: the model starts to read them as advice.
s18.t05: Rules in capitals with no reason: every rule carries its reason.
s18.t06: A stray file (if your skill has several files): the main text never mentions it; mention it or delete the file.
s18.t07: Old versions inside the skill: the log of edits lives elsewhere.
s18.t08: A “fine” mark that does not say what was inspected.
s18.t09: Before sharing: five elements in place, no more than six rules, 3–5 runs passed, defects hunted by someone other than the author.
s19.t02: Versions and care: a skill lives while it is looked after
s19.t03: Versions: a skill has a number (1.0, 1.1…); change it with every edit. Write the number as a line “Version: 1.0” right after the description, not inside it.
s19.t04: A review on a schedule: remove what is outdated, add what failures showed.
s19.t05: Cleaning: keep only what the skill needs to work; store old versions elsewhere.
s19.t06: Sharing: after an independent audit and test runs.
s19.t07: The first version carries the minimum rules for your two or three cases; real failures add the rest.
s20.t09: Leads you from a task to a finished skill.
s20.t12: Two files and a note on how to run them.
